claim: Cytosine DNA methylation (mC) is a genome modification that can regulate the expression of coding and non-coding genetic elements.
source: Cytosine DNA methylation (mC) is a genome modification that can regulate the expression of coding and non-coding genetic elements.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about DNA methylation function.

claim: Phosphate starvation induces widespread changes in DNA methylation in rice, preferentially localized in transposable elements (TEs) close to highly induced genes.
source: Using whole genome bisulfite sequencing to assess the spatio-temporal dynamics of mC in rice grown under phosphate starvation and recovery conditions, we identified widespread phosphate starvation-induced changes in mC, preferentially localized in transposable elements (TEs) close to highly induced genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by whole genome bisulfite sequencing data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Changes in DNA methylation occurred after changes in nearby gene transcription in response to phosphate starvation.
source: These changes in mC occurred after changes in nearby gene transcription, were mostly DCL3a-independent, and could partially be propagated through mitosis, however no evidence of meiotic transmission was observed.
evidence: This is supported by temporal analysis of transcription and methylation data across multiple time points.

claim: Phosphate starvation-induced changes in DNA methylation are mostly DCL3a-independent.
source: These changes in mC occurred after changes in nearby gene transcription, were mostly DCL3a-independent, and could partially be propagated through mitosis, however no evidence of meiotic transmission was observed.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of methylation changes in wild-type and DCL3a RNAi plants.

claim: Phosphate starvation-induced changes in DNA methylation could partially be propagated through mitosis.
source: These changes in mC occurred after changes in nearby gene transcription, were mostly DCL3a-independent, and could partially be propagated through mitosis, however no evidence of meiotic transmission was observed.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of methylation patterns during recovery periods with active cell growth.

claim: No evidence of meiotic transmission of phosphate starvation-induced DNA methylation changes was observed.
source: These changes in mC occurred after changes in nearby gene transcription, were mostly DCL3a-independent, and could partially be propagated through mitosis, however no evidence of meiotic transmission was observed.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of methylation patterns in progeny of stressed plants.

claim: Phosphate starvation has a very limited effect on DNA methylation in Arabidopsis.
source: Similar analyses performed in Arabidopsis revealed a very limited effect of phosphate starvation on mC, suggesting a species-specific mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by whole genome bisulfite sequencing data from Arabidopsis under phosphate starvation.

claim: The effect of phosphate starvation on DNA methylation is species-specific.
source: Similar analyses performed in Arabidopsis revealed a very limited effect of phosphate starvation on mC, suggesting a species-specific mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of rice and Arabidopsis methylation responses to phosphate starvation.

claim: TEs in proximity to environmentally induced genes are silenced via hypermethylation in response to stress.
source: Overall, this suggests that TEs in proximity to environmentally induced genes are silenced via hypermethylation, and establishes the temporal hierarchy of transcriptional and epigenomic changes in response to stress.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that hypermethylated DMRs overlap with TEs near stress-induced genes.

claim: Phosphorus (P) is one of the most important macronutrients for all living organisms.
source: Phosphorus (P) is one of the most important macronutrients for all living organisms, being a key component of nucleic acids and membrane phospholipids, as well as being an essential element for energy-mediated metabolic processes.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about phosphorus.

claim: Phosphorus is a key component of nucleic acids and membrane phospholipids.
source: Phosphorus (P) is one of the most important macronutrients for all living organisms, being a key component of nucleic acids and membrane phospholipids, as well as being an essential element for energy-mediated metabolic processes.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about phosphorus biochemistry.

claim: Phosphorus is an essential element for energy-mediated metabolic processes.
source: Phosphorus (P) is one of the most important macronutrients for all living organisms, being a key component of nucleic acids and membrane phospholipids, as well as being an essential element for energy-mediated metabolic processes.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about phosphorus in metabolism.

claim: Plants preferentially absorb phosphorus as inorganic phosphate (Pi).
source: Plants preferentially absorb this nutrient as inorganic phosphate (Pi), a form of P with low availability and mobility in the soil (Poirier and Bucher, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Inorganic phosphate has low availability and mobility in the soil.
source: Plants preferentially absorb this nutrient as inorganic phosphate (Pi), a form of P with low availability and mobility in the soil (Poirier and Bucher, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Pi is one of the most limiting nutrients for plant growth and development in most agricultural soils.
source: As a consequence, Pi is one of the most limiting nutrients for plant growth and development in most agricultural soils.
evidence: This is inferred from the low availability of Pi in soils and is established agricultural knowledge.

claim: 21 days of Pi deprivation resulted in a 2.3 fold decrease in shoot biomass.
source: Growth analyses revealed that 21 days of Pi deprivation resulted in a 2.3 fold decrease in shoot biomass (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is supported by growth measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: No significant differences in root biomass were observed after 21 days of Pi deprivation.
source: however no significant differences could be observed for the root biomass after 21 days of treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by growth measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Plants grown under Pi deficient conditions for 21 days showed a 2.2 fold increase in root-to-shoot biomass ratio compared to plants grown under Pi sufficient conditions.
source: Consequently, the root-to-shoot biomass ratio, a parameter often used to assess the efficiency of various nutrient stresses, was significantly altered (t-test, p < 0.05), with plants grown under Pi deficient conditions for 21 days showing a 2.2 fold increase compared to plants grown under Pi sufficient conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This is supported by calculated ratios from biomass measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The root-to-shoot biomass ratio is a parameter often used to assess the efficiency of various nutrient stresses.
source: Consequently, the root-to-shoot biomass ratio, a parameter often used to assess the efficiency of various nutrient stresses, was significantly altered (t-test, p < 0.05)
evidence: This is established knowledge in plant stress physiology.

claim: 3 days of Pi deprivation led to a threefold reduction in root Pi concentration.
source: Pi concentration measurements revealed that 3 days of −Pi led to a threefold reduction in root Pi concentration, while 21 days −Pi resulted in a 6 fold decrease in root Pi concentration compared to plants continuously grown under Pi sufficient conditions (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by Pi concentration measurements shown in Figure 1C.

claim: 21 days of Pi deprivation resulted in a 6 fold decrease in root Pi concentration compared to plants continuously grown under Pi sufficient conditions.
source: Pi concentration measurements revealed that 3 days of −Pi led to a threefold reduction in root Pi concentration, while 21 days −Pi resulted in a 6 fold decrease in root Pi concentration compared to plants continuously grown under Pi sufficient conditions (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by Pi concentration measurements shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Resupplying Pi for 1 day was sufficient to increase the root Pi concentration >4 fold compared to plants grown under Pi deficient conditions.
source: Resupplying Pi for 1 day was sufficient to increase the root Pi concentration >4 fold compared to plants grown under Pi deficient conditions, and within 3 days of Pi resupply the root Pi concentration was similar to that of plants continuously grown under Pi sufficient conditions.
evidence: This is supported by Pi concentration measurements.

claim: Within 3 days of Pi resupply the root Pi concentration was similar to that of plants continuously grown under Pi sufficient conditions.
source: Resupplying Pi for 1 day was sufficient to increase the root Pi concentration >4 fold compared to plants grown under Pi deficient conditions, and within 3 days of Pi resupply the root Pi concentration was similar to that of plants continuously grown under Pi sufficient conditions.
evidence: This is supported by Pi concentration measurements.

claim: 5570 genes were identified as significantly differentially expressed in at least one of the time points in response to Pi starvation.
source: Hierarchical clustering of the steady state transcript abundance of the 5570 genes identified as significantly differentially expressed (Cuffdiff, FDR < 0.05) in at least one of the time points revealed a gradual increase in the number and fold change of differentially expressed genes upon −Pi, associated with the length of the Pi deprivation (Figure 1D,E; Figure 1—source data 1, available at Dryad, Secco et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: There was a gradual increase in the number and fold change of differentially expressed genes upon Pi deprivation, associated with the length of the Pi deprivation.
source: Hierarchical clustering of the steady state transcript abundance of the 5570 genes identified as significantly differentially expressed (Cuffdiff, FDR < 0.05) in at least one of the time points revealed a gradual increase in the number and fold change of differentially expressed genes upon −Pi, associated with the length of the Pi deprivation (Figure 1D,E; Figure 1—source data 1, available at Dryad, Secco et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: Several phosphate starvation-induced (PSI) marker genes, including the SPX genes, MGD2 and PTs, were already induced and showed high steady state transcript abundance after only 3 days of Pi deprivation.
source: Of note, several phosphate starvation-induced (PSI) marker genes, including the SPX genes, MGD2 and PTs, were already induced and showed high steady state transcript abundance after only 3 days of Pi deprivation (Figure 1—source data 1, available at Dryad, Secco et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data in Figure 1—source data 1.

claim: Resupplying Pi for 1 day after 21 days of starvation was sufficient for the transcript abundance of 40% of PSI differentially regulated genes to return to a level that was not significantly different from the +Pi condition at the matched time point.
source: Resupplying Pi for 1 day after 21 days of starvation was sufficient for the transcript abundance of 40% of PSI differentially regulated genes to return to a level that was not significantly different from the +Pi condition at the matched time point (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: Within 3 days of Pi resupply, the transcript abundance of 80% of the 5570 PSI differentially expressed genes had already returned to levels equivalent to Pi sufficient conditions.
source: Within 3 days of Pi resupply, the internal root Pi content was similar to that of Pi sufficient plants and the transcript abundance of 80% of the 5570 PSI differentially expressed genes had already returned to levels equivalent to Pi sufficient conditions.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis.

claim: After 31 days of Pi resupply, the transcript abundance of only 80 PSI genes remained significantly different compared to Pi sufficient conditions.
source: After 31 days of Pi resupply, the transcript abundance of only 80 PSI genes remained significantly different compared to Pi sufficient conditions.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis.

claim: 175 high confidence root PSI DMRs were identified in rice.
source: The methylation levels in all sequence contexts (CNN) were then assessed for these samples, and only regions that showed significant differences in methylation levels (FDR < 0.01) in at least 7 of the 9 samples in each of the conditions were considered for further analysis, resulting in the identification of 175 high confidence root PSI DMRs (Figure 2—source data 1, available at Dryad, Secco et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by MethylC-seq analysis.

claim: 84% of the 175 PSI DMRs were hypermethylated in response to Pi starvation.
source: Among these 175 PSI DMRs, 84% were hypermethylated in response to Pi starvation (147 hypermethylated, 28 hypomethylated regions, Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by MethylC-seq analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The root PSI DMRs had an average size of 205 bp with a mean of 16 differentially methylated cytosines per DMR.
source: The root PSI DMRs had an average size of 205 bp with a mean of 16 differentially methylated cytosines per DMR, and were preferentially localized within the first two kilobases upstream (40%) and first kilobase downstream (15%) of the nearby gene (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of DMR characteristics shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Root PSI DMRs were preferentially localized within the first two kilobases upstream (40%) and first kilobase downstream (15%) of the nearby gene.
source: The root PSI DMRs had an average size of 205 bp with a mean of 16 differentially methylated cytosines per DMR, and were preferentially localized within the first two kilobases upstream (40%) and first kilobase downstream (15%) of the nearby gene (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of DMR positions shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 90% of the 175 root PSI DMRs overlapped with TEs.
source: Among the 175 root PSI DMRs, 90% overlapped with TEs, with Miniature Inverted-repeat Transposable Elements (MITEs), the most common class of TEs in the rice genome (69% of all TEs), accounting for 58% of the DMRs overlapping with TEs (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Miniature Inverted-repeat Transposable Elements (MITEs) are the most common class of TEs in the rice genome, accounting for 69% of all TEs.
source: Among the 175 root PSI DMRs, 90% overlapped with TEs, with Miniature Inverted-repeat Transposable Elements (MITEs), the most common class of TEs in the rice genome (69% of all TEs), accounting for 58% of the DMRs overlapping with TEs (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is established knowledge about rice genome composition.

claim: MITEs accounted for 58% of the DMRs overlapping with TEs.
source: Among the 175 root PSI DMRs, 90% overlapped with TEs, with Miniature Inverted-repeat Transposable Elements (MITEs), the most common class of TEs in the rice genome (69% of all TEs), accounting for 58% of the DMRs overlapping with TEs (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: More than 80% of TEs overlapping with PSI DMRs were not expressed.
source: In addition, RNA-seq analysis failed to reveal any significantly differentially expressed TEs (Cuffdiff, FDR < 0.05) that overlapped with PSI DMRs, between Pi sufficient and deficient conditions (7 and 21 days), with more than 80% of them not being expressed (Figure 2—source data 2, available at Dryad, Secco et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis of TEs.

claim: 126 unique genes were associated with the 175 PSI DMRs.
source: Next, each of the 175 PSI DMRs were assigned to the nearest gene, resulting in the association of 126 unique genes with PSI DMRs (Figure 2—source data 1, available at Dryad, Secco et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by gene assignment analysis.

claim: 66 of the 126 DMR-associated genes (52%) were differentially expressed by >2 fold in response to 21 days Pi deprivation.
source: Gene transcript abundance analyses revealed that 66 of these DMR-associated genes (52%) were differentially expressed by >2 fold (FDR < 0.05) in response to 21 days −Pi (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The steady state transcript abundance of 35% of the 126 DMR-associated genes was >4 fold higher following 21 days Pi starvation.
source: The steady state transcript abundance of 35% of the 126 genes was >4 fold higher following 21 days Pi starvation.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis.

claim: DMR-associated genes showed strong enrichment for genes encoding proteins involved in phosphate homeostasis.
source: Furthermore, gene ontology analyses revealed a strong enrichment for genes encoding proteins involved in phosphate homeostasis, such as acid phosphatases, phosphate transporters, and factors involved in glycerophosphodiester phosphodiesterase activity (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: 341 shoot PSI DMRs were identified in rice.
source: Secondly, shoot methylomes under Pi-sufficient and deficient conditions were analysed in order to identify shoot PSI DMRs. Due to the lower number of replicates used to identify shoot PSI DMRs (n = 3) compared to the root PSI DMRs (n = 9), a less stringent FDR cut-off of < 0.05 was selected for further analysis, resulting in the identification of 341 shoot PSI DMRs (FDR < 0.05) (Figure 2—source data 3, available at Dryad, Secco et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by MethylC-seq analysis of shoot samples.

claim: 43 distinct genes were significantly differentially regulated by Pi starvation in the shoots.
source: Assigning the 341 shoot PSI DMRs to the nearest genes identified 43 distinct genes that were significantly differentially regulated by Pi starvation in the shoots (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by gene assignment and RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: More than 30 conserved regions showed significant changes in both roots and shoots.
source: Altogether, more than 30 conserved regions showed significant changes in both roots and shoots, and could be associated to PSI marker genes such as SPX1, SPX2 and MGD2.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of root and shoot methylation data.

claim: 100 PSI DMRs were close to genes showing significant changes in gene transcription upon long term Pi starvation.
source: Among the 175 root PSI DMRs identified, 100 PSI DMRs were close to genes showing significant changes (FDR < 0.05) in gene transcription upon long term Pi starvation, corresponding to 66 unique genes (Figure 3A, Figure 2—source data 1, available at Dryad, Secco et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by integration of methylation and transcription data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: 63 (95%) of the 66 DMR-associated genes were induced by Pi starvation.
source: Notably, 63 (95%) of these DMR-associated genes were induced by Pi starvation, and included key regulators of Pi homeostasis such as Pi transporters (PT3, PT4, PT9, PT10), SPX genes (SPX1, SPX2, SPX3, SPX5), MGD2, IPS1 and pre-miR827.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis.

claim: Only three of the DMR-associated genes were down-regulated by long term Pi starvation.
source: Only three of the DMR-associated genes were down-regulated by long term Pi starvation.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis.

claim: 81 PSI DMRs associated with 61 genes were overwhelmingly hypermethylated in the CHH context.
source: The first group contained 81 PSI DMRs associated with 61 genes that were overwhelmingly hypermethylated in the CHH context, with a subset displaying CHG hypermethylation.
evidence: This is supported by context-specific methylation analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: 80 of 81 hypermethylated PSI DMRs overlapped with TEs.
source: Furthermore, these hypermethylated DMRs almost exclusively (80 of 81) overlapped with TEs (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: 19 hypomethylated PSI DMRs were associated with 13 unique genes.
source: In contrast, the 19 hypomethylated PSI DMRs from Cluster 2, associated with 13 unique genes, less frequently overlapped with TEs (42% overlap).
evidence: This is supported by clustering and overlap analysis.

claim: 42% of hypomethylated PSI DMRs overlapped with TEs.
source: In contrast, the 19 hypomethylated PSI DMRs from Cluster 2, associated with 13 unique genes, less frequently overlapped with TEs (42% overlap).
evidence: This is supported by overlap analysis.

claim: After 3 days of Pi starvation, 18% of the PSI DMR associated genes showed significant changes in transcript abundance.
source: After 3 and 7 days of Pi starvation, 18% and 55% of the PSI DMR associated genes, respectively, showed significant changes in transcript abundance (Cuffdiff, FDR < 0.05), while only 5% and 9% of the 100 PSI DMRs showed significant changes in DNA methylation compared to +Pi samples (t-test, FDR < 0.05) (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—source data 1, available at Dryad, Secco et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by temporal analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: After 7 days of Pi starvation, 55% of the PSI DMR associated genes showed significant changes in transcript abundance.
source: After 3 and 7 days of Pi starvation, 18% and 55% of the PSI DMR associated genes, respectively, showed significant changes in transcript abundance (Cuffdiff, FDR < 0.05), while only 5% and 9% of the 100 PSI DMRs showed significant changes in DNA methylation compared to +Pi samples (t-test, FDR < 0.05) (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—source data 1, available at Dryad, Secco et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by temporal analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: After 3 days of Pi starvation, only 5% of the 100 PSI DMRs showed significant changes in DNA methylation compared to +Pi samples.
source: After 3 and 7 days of Pi starvation, 18% and 55% of the PSI DMR associated genes, respectively, showed significant changes in transcript abundance (Cuffdiff, FDR < 0.05), while only 5% and 9% of the 100 PSI DMRs showed significant changes in DNA methylation compared to +Pi samples (t-test, FDR < 0.05) (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—source data 1, available at Dryad, Secco et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by temporal analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: After 7 days of Pi starvation, 9% of the 100 PSI DMRs showed significant changes in DNA methylation compared to +Pi samples.
source: After 3 and 7 days of Pi starvation, 18% and 55% of the PSI DMR associated genes, respectively, showed significant changes in transcript abundance (Cuffdiff, FDR < 0.05), while only 5% and 9% of the 100 PSI DMRs showed significant changes in DNA methylation compared to +Pi samples (t-test, FDR < 0.05) (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—source data 1, available at Dryad, Secco et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by temporal analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: All PSI DMRs were significantly differentially methylated after 24 days of Pi deprivation compared to +Pi.
source: Long term Pi deprivation (≥21 days −Pi) was sufficient to induce significant changes in both gene transcript abundance and DNA methylation levels, with all PSI DMRs being significantly differentially methylated after 24 days of −Pi compared to +Pi (t-test, FDR < 0.05).
evidence: This is supported by temporal methylation analysis.

claim: Resupplying Pi starved plants with Pi for 3 days resulted in 87% of the DMR associated genes differentially expressed upon Pi starvation to return to Pi sufficient-like levels.
source: Furthermore, while resupplying Pi starved plants with Pi for 3 days resulted in 87% of the DMR associated genes differentially expressed upon Pi starvation to return to Pi sufficient-like levels, 94% of PSI DMRs still showed significant differences in DNA methylation levels compared to +Pi conditions (t-test, FDR < 0.05).
evidence: This is supported by temporal analysis of transcription and methylation during recovery.

claim: After 3 days of Pi resupply, 94% of PSI DMRs still showed significant differences in DNA methylation levels compared to +Pi conditions.
source: Furthermore, while resupplying Pi starved plants with Pi for 3 days resulted in 87% of the DMR associated genes differentially expressed upon Pi starvation to return to Pi sufficient-like levels, 94% of PSI DMRs still showed significant differences in DNA methylation levels compared to +Pi conditions (t-test, FDR < 0.05).
evidence: This is supported by temporal analysis of methylation during recovery.

claim: After 52 days of Pi starvation, only 22% of PSI DMR associated genes showed significant changes in transcript abundance compared to +Pi.
source: Finally, while 52 days of Pi starvation resulted in only 22% of PSI DMR associated genes showing significant changes in transcript abundance (Cuffdiff, FDR < 0.05) compared to +Pi, likely a consequence of the floral transition and nutrient reallocation to the grains, the majority of PSI DMRs remained unaffected, with 83% of PSI DMRs still showing significant changes in DNA methylation after 52 days −Pi compared to 52 days +Pi (t-test, FDR < 0.05).
evidence: This is supported by long-term temporal analysis.

claim: After 52 days of Pi starvation, 83% of PSI DMRs still showed significant changes in DNA methylation compared to 52 days +Pi.
source: Finally, while 52 days of Pi starvation resulted in only 22% of PSI DMR associated genes showing significant changes in transcript abundance (Cuffdiff, FDR < 0.05) compared to +Pi, likely a consequence of the floral transition and nutrient reallocation to the grains, the majority of PSI DMRs remained unaffected, with 83% of PSI DMRs still showing significant changes in DNA methylation after 52 days −Pi compared to 52 days +Pi (t-test, FDR < 0.05).
evidence: This is supported by long-term temporal analysis.

claim: Resupplying Pi for 31 days resulted in 11 of the 100 PSI DMRs showing significant persisting changes in DNA methylation while no significant changes in gene transcription could be observed compared to +Pi.
source: Resupplying Pi for 31 days resulted in 11 of the 100 PSI DMRs showing significant persisting changes in DNA methylation (t-test, FDR < 0.05) while no significant changes in gene transcription could be observed compared to +Pi.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of methylation and transcription after extended recovery.

claim: 96 of the 175 PSI DMRs showed more than a 2 fold reduction in the differential DNA methylation levels induced by 52 days Pi deprivation after 31 days of Pi resupply.
source: However, resupplying Pi for 31 days resulted in 96 of the 175 PSI DMRs showing more than a 2 fold reduction in the differential DNA methylation levels induced by 52 days −Pi, when compared to +Pi, suggesting that the majority of PSI DMRs are returning towards Pi sufficient levels after 31 days of Pi resupply (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only 14 of the 175 PSI DMRs showed significant differences in DNA methylation level between 52 days +Pi compared to 52 days resupply.
source: Indeed, only 14 of the 175 PSI DMRs (11 hypermethylated, 3 hypomethylated) showed significant differences in DNA methylation level (CNN) between 52 days +Pi compared to 52 days resupply (t-test, FDR < 0.05), while not presenting significant differences between 52 days −Pi vs 52 days resupply (t-test, FDR > 0.05), suggesting that changes in DNA methylation persist in only a limited subset of these PSI DMRs after 31 days of Pi resupply (Figure 4A, Figure 4—source data 1, available at Dryad, Secco et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Persistent differences in methylation levels preferentially occurred in the CHH context.
source: These persistent differences in methylation levels preferentially occurred in the CHH context (Figure 4A) and were associated with 13 unique genes located nearby, including key regulators of Pi homeostasis such as SPX2 and MGD2.
evidence: This is supported by context-specific analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: 36 PSI DMRs were induced by 52 days of Pi deprivation in the panicles.
source: Generation of high coverage methylomes enabled the identification of 36 PSI DMRs in the panicles of plants grown for 52 days in +Pi and −Pi (FDR < 0.05).
evidence: This is supported by MethylC-seq analysis of panicle tissue.

claim: No significant differences could be observed in the DNA methylation levels of the 36 panicle PSI DMRs between panicles of plants grown for 52 days in −Pi compared to those resupplied with Pi for 31 days.
source: However, no significant differences (t-test, FDR < 0.05) could be observed in the DNA methylation levels of these 36 regions between panicles of plants grown for 52 days in −Pi compared to those resupplied with Pi for 31 days (Figure 4B, Figure 4—source data 2, available at Dryad, Secco et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Analysis of the methylation levels in the progeny of stressed and non-stressed parents in the 175 root PSI DMRs failed to identify any significant differences in DNA methylation levels.
source: Analysis of the methylation levels in the progeny of stressed and non-stressed parents in the 175 root PSI DMRs that were identified in the first generation of plants failed to identify any significant differences in DNA methylation levels (t-test, FDR < 0.05) (Figure 4C,D,E, Figure 4—figure supplement 2, Figure 4—source data 3, available at Dryad, Secco et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of progeny methylomes shown in Figure 4C,D,E.

claim: Independent of the treatment performed in the parental generation, DNA methylation levels were reset to a Pi-sufficient like level in the progeny.
source: Indeed, independent of the treatment performed in the parental generation, DNA methylation levels were reset to a Pi-sufficient like level in the progeny (Figure 4C,D,E, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of progeny methylomes shown in Figure 4C,D,E.

claim: DCL3a is the most abundant DCL3 family member in the roots, with 11 times higher steady state transcript abundance than DCL3b under Pi sufficient conditions.
source: RNA-seq analysis (n = 3) confirmed that DCL3a was the most abundant DCL3 family member in the roots, with 11 times higher steady state transcript abundance than DCL3b under Pi sufficient conditions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A; Figure 5—source data1, available at Dryad, Secco et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In the DCL3a RNAi line, the transcript abundance of DCL3a decreased by 4.6 and 3.3 fold compared to WT in Pi sufficient or deficient conditions, respectively.
source: In the DCL3a RNAi line, the transcript abundance of DCL3a decreased by 4.6 and 3.3 fold compared to WT in Pi sufficient or deficient conditions, respectively, while the abundance of DCL3b transcript was unaffected (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B, Figure 5—source data1, available at Dryad, Secco et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The abundance of DCL3b transcript was unaffected in the DCL3a RNAi line.
source: In the DCL3a RNAi line, the transcript abundance of DCL3a decreased by 4.6 and 3.3 fold compared to WT in Pi sufficient or deficient conditions, respectively, while the abundance of DCL3b transcript was unaffected (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B, Figure 5—source data1, available at Dryad, Secco et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: In +Pi conditions, the reduced transcription of DCL3a was accompanied by widespread changes in DNA methylation, significantly altering DNA methylation levels in 9379 regions in the genome.
source: In +Pi conditions, the reduced transcription of DCL3a was accompanied by widespread changes in DNA methylation, significantly altering DNA methylation levels in 9379 regions in the genome (6694 hypo- and 2685 hypermethylated regions in DCL3a RNAi line compared to WT; FDR < 0.05), in addition to 3531 genes displaying a significant change in transcript abundance (Cuffdiff, FDR < 0.05) compared to WT +Pi (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of WT and DCL3a RNAi methylomes shown in Figure 5A.

claim: 3531 genes displayed a significant change in transcript abundance in DCL3a RNAi line compared to WT under +Pi conditions.
source: In +Pi conditions, the reduced transcription of DCL3a was accompanied by widespread changes in DNA methylation, significantly altering DNA methylation levels in 9379 regions in the genome (6694 hypo- and 2685 hypermethylated regions in DCL3a RNAi line compared to WT; FDR < 0.05), in addition to 3531 genes displaying a significant change in transcript abundance (Cuffdiff, FDR < 0.05) compared to WT +Pi (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq comparison shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Under Pi deficient conditions, 8164 DMRs and 1791 differentially expressed genes were identified between WT and DCL3a RNAi plants.
source: Similar results were also observed between WT and DCL3a RNAi plants under Pi deficient conditions, with 8164 DMRs and 1791 differentially expressed genes identified (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, Figure 5—source data 1, available at Dryad, Secco et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of WT and DCL3a RNAi under -Pi shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The majority of changes in DNA methylation in DCL3a RNAi plants occurred in the CG and CHG contexts, under both Pi sufficient and deficient conditions.
source: Analysis of the DMRs induced in DCL3a RNAi plants revealed that the majority of changes in DNA methylation occurred in the CG and CHG contexts, under both Pi sufficient and deficient conditions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,E,F,G).
evidence: This is supported by context-specific analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,E,F,G.

claim: Among the 175 PSI DMRs, only 8 and 5 regions showed significant differences in DNA methylation between WT and DCL3a plants under Pi sufficient and deficient conditions, respectively.
source: Among the 175 PSI DMRs identified previously (Figure 2A), only 8 and 5 regions also showed significant differences in DNA methylation between WT and DCL3a plants under Pi sufficient and deficient conditions, respectively, and corresponded to 11 unique PSI DMRs (8 unique associated genes) (Figure 5A,B,C,D; Figure 5—source data 2, available at Dryad, Secco et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 5A,B,C,D.

claim: DNA methylation was almost completely abolished in all contexts in five hypomethylated PSI DMRs in DCL3a RNAi plants, which were associated with SPX1, SPX2 and MGD2.
source: Furthermore, while reduction in DCL3a transcript levels only moderately affected DNA methylation in 6 of the 11 PSI DMRs (mC change < 15%), DNA methylation was almost completely abolished in all contexts in five of these hypomethylated PSI DMRs, which were associated with SPX1, SPX2 and MGD2 (Figure 5D,E,F).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 5D,E,F.

claim: Three DMRs associated with SPX2 showed an average reduction in DNA methylation levels from 47% in WT +Pi to 1% in DCL3a RNAi plants +Pi.
source: Among these, three DMRs were associated with SPX2, and showed an average reduction in DNA methylation levels from 47% in WT +Pi to 1% in DCL3a RNAi plants +Pi, indicating a requirement for DCL3a in maintaining the methylation in these regions (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 5E,F.

claim: Among the 8 genes associated with DCL3a-dependant PSI DMRs, only SPX2 showed significant changes in transcript abundance between WT and DCL3a RNAi plants.
source: Furthermore, among the 8 genes associated with DCL3a-dependant PSI DMRs, only SPX2 showed significant changes in transcript abundance between WT and DCL3a RNAi plants, decreasing by 69 fold under +Pi conditions (15.9 FPKM in WT +Pi and 0.2 FPKM in DCL3a RNAi plants +Pi) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1H.

claim: SPX2 transcript abundance decreased by 69 fold in DCL3a RNAi plants compared to WT under +Pi conditions.
source: Furthermore, among the 8 genes associated with DCL3a-dependant PSI DMRs, only SPX2 showed significant changes in transcript abundance between WT and DCL3a RNAi plants, decreasing by 69 fold under +Pi conditions (15.9 FPKM in WT +Pi and 0.2 FPKM in DCL3a RNAi plants +Pi) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1H.

claim: 409 PSI DMRs were identified in the stressed DCL3a RNAi plants.
source: Together, 409 PSI DMRs (FDR < 0.05) were identified in the stressed DCL3a RNAi plants (Figure 5—figure supplement 2, Figure 5—source data 3, available at Dryad, Secco et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by DMR analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: 4560 genes displayed differential transcript abundance in Arabidopsis roots after 10 days of Pi starvation.
source: RNA-seq analysis was performed to assess the transcriptional response to the Pi treatments, identifying 4560 genes displaying differential transcript abundance in the roots after 10 days of Pi starvation (Cuffdiff, FDR < 0.05) (Figure 6A, Figure 6—source data 1, available at Dryad, Secco et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Known PSI marker genes such as SPX3, IPS1, miR399 and PHT1;9 showed >100 fold higher transcript abundance upon Pi starvation in Arabidopsis.
source: Known PSI marker genes such as SPX3, IPS1, miR399 and PHT1;9 showed >100 fold higher transcript abundance upon Pi starvation.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis.

claim: Of the 4560 PSI genes that displayed differential transcript abundance by 10 days of Pi deprivation in Arabidopsis, only 10% showed significantly different transcript abundance after 3 days of resupply compared to +Pi.
source: In addition, resupplying Pi for 3 days was sufficient for the transcript abundance of the majority of the PSI genes to return to +Pi like levels. Indeed, of the 4560 PSI genes that displayed differential transcript abundance by 10 days of −Pi, only 10% showed significantly different transcript abundance after 3 days of resupply compared to +Pi.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis during recovery.

claim: Two PSI DMRs were identified in Arabidopsis using FDR < 0.2.
source: While no PSI DMRs could be detected using a FDR < 0.05, two PSI DMRs were identified using lower stringency parameters (FDR < 0.2), requiring only two of the three replicates to show significant methylation differences for each condition.
evidence: This is supported by MethylC-seq analysis of Arabidopsis.

claim: The two Arabidopsis PSI DMRs were associated with MGD3 and Atcopeg1.
source: Assignment of these DMRs to the nearest gene revealed that they were associated with two known PSI genes, MGD3, encoding for the major enzyme for galactolipid metabolism during phosphate starvation (Kobayashi et al., 2009), and Atcopeg1 (Copia evolved gene 1), the only expressed gene derived from the AtCopia95 retrotransposon in the Arabidopsis genome, which has been shown to be involved in many developmental and adaptive processes, including Pi starvation (Duan et al., 2008) (Figure 6B,D).
evidence: This is supported by gene assignment and citations to prior research.

claim: For both Arabidopsis PSI DMRs, resupplying Pi for 3 days resulted in a significant reduction in the CHG and CHH methylation levels compared to −Pi.
source: For both DMRs, resupplying Pi for 3 days resulted in a significant reduction in the CHG and CHH methylation levels compared to −Pi (Figure 6C,E).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 6C,E.

claim: Under Pi sufficient conditions only 10% of the cytosines in the CHH context were methylated in the DMR associated with Atcopeg1.
source: For example, while under Pi sufficient conditions only 10% of the cytosines in the CHH context were methylated in the DMR associated with Atcopeg1, Pi starvation increased the number of methylated cytosines in the CHH context to 40%, before returning to 24% upon 3 days of Pi resupply, suggesting that the changes in DNA methylation observed are transient.
evidence: This is supported by methylation analysis of the Atcopeg1 DMR.

claim: Pi starvation increased the number of methylated cytosines in the CHH context in the Atcopeg1 DMR to 40%.
source: For example, while under Pi sufficient conditions only 10% of the cytosines in the CHH context were methylated in the DMR associated with Atcopeg1, Pi starvation increased the number of methylated cytosines in the CHH context to 40%, before returning to 24% upon 3 days of Pi resupply, suggesting that the changes in DNA methylation observed are transient.
evidence: This is supported by methylation analysis of the Atcopeg1 DMR.

claim: The methylation in the Atcopeg1 DMR returned to 24% upon 3 days of Pi resupply.
source: For example, while under Pi sufficient conditions only 10% of the cytosines in the CHH context were methylated in the DMR associated with Atcopeg1, Pi starvation increased the number of methylated cytosines in the CHH context to 40%, before returning to 24% upon 3 days of Pi resupply, suggesting that the changes in DNA methylation observed are transient.
evidence: This is supported by methylation analysis of the Atcopeg1 DMR.

claim: The differences in DNA methylation changes observed in rice and Arabidopsis in response to Pi starvation could primarily be due to the differential frequency of TEs in the genome of each species.
source: Potentially, the differences in DNA methylation changes observed in rice and Arabidopsis in response to Pi starvation could primarily be due to the differential frequency of TEs in the genome of each species.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed differences and known TE content.

claim: The TE-rich genome (∼40%) of rice has a much higher aggregate level of DNA methylation than the TE-poor (∼15%) Arabidopsis genome.
source: Indeed, the TE-rich genome (∼40%) of rice has a much higher aggregate level of DNA methylation than the TE-poor (∼15%) Arabidopsis genome (Li et al., 2012; Ragupathy et al., 2013; Mirouze and Vitte, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: DNA methylation exists in all sequence contexts (CG, CHG, CHH) in plants through the activity of multiple genetically distinct pathways.
source: In plants, DNA methylation exists in all sequence contexts (CG, CHG, CHH, where H = A, C or T) through the activity of multiple genetically distinct pathways (Law and Jacobsen, 2010; Matzke and Mosher, 2014; Mirouze and Vitte, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: De novo DNA methylation is mediated by the RNA-directed DNA methylation (RdDM) pathways.
source: De novo DNA methylation is mediated by the RNA-directed DNA methylation (RdDM) pathways.
evidence: This is established knowledge about DNA methylation mechanisms.

claim: The RDR6-RdDM pathway is independent of Pol IV and DCL3.
source: Recently, another RdDM pathway, which is independent of Pol IV and DCL3, has been identified and is referred to as RDR6-RdDM (Nuthikattu et al., 2013; Panda and Slotkin, 2013; Creasey et al., 2014; Matzke and Mosher, 2014; Bond and Baulcombe, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The RDR6-RdDM pathway may act to methylate TEs near highly induced PSI genes.
source: This hypothesis is strengthened by the fact that the majority of the hypermethylated PSI DMRs are independent of DCL3a, a key component of the canonical RdDM pathway. Thus, we hypothesize that the RDR6-RdDM pathway, another entry point into RdDM that recognizes Pol II-derived TE transcripts, may act to methylate these TEs.
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from the DCL3a-independence of most hypermethylated DMRs.

claim: The observed increase in DNA methylation in specific TEs located close to PSI genes may act to maintain localized suppression of transposable elements in genomic regions that must be transcriptionally activated to respond to environmental perturbation.
source: Overall, the observed increase in DNA methylation in specific TEs located close to PSI genes provides insights into a cellular activity that may act to maintain localized suppression of transposable elements in genomic regions that must be transcriptionally activated to respond to environmental perturbation (Figure 7).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data supported by the model in Figure 7.
